Palo Alto Networks Patches PAN-OS Authenticated RCE Flaw Amid Active Exploitation
thehackernews.com · 15 Oct 2026 06:17 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGScisaciscocisco-secure-email-gatewaycloud-ngfwcve-2026-0322cve-2026-76519pa-seriespalo-alto-networkspan-ospanoramaprisma-accessremote-code-executionunited-statesvm-series
95
In plain words

Palo Alto Networks released fixes for a flaw in the software that manages some of its firewalls, and the company says attackers have already made limited attempts to use it. Someone who already has authorized access to a device’s management page could use the flaw to take full control of the firewall. The issue affects PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama management systems, so organizations using them should install the available updates and limit who can reach the management page.

Summary
Palo Alto Networks patched CVE-2026-0322, an actively exploited authenticated PAN-OS management-interface flaw that can grant attackers root-level remote code execution. Organizations should urgently upgrade affected PA-Series, VM-Series, and Panorama systems and restrict management access to trusted internal hosts.

Palo Alto Networks released security updates for CVE-2026-0322, a high-severity PAN-OS flaw with a CVSS score of 8.6 that has seen very limited active exploitation. The issue affects the management interface of PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama virtual and M-Series systems. An authenticated attacker with network access can use it to run arbitrary code with root privileges on an affected firewall. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected.

Palo Alto Networks said no special configuration is necessary to exploit the flaw and advised restricting management-interface access to trusted internal IP addresses or a jump box. Fixes are available across specified PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2 release versions, with PAN-OS 11.2.16 listed as expected on October 15, 2026. The company identified three U.S.-geolocated IP addresses assessed as linked to exploit attempts. CISA added CVE-2026-0322 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and required U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to prioritize fixes by October 17, 2026.

  • The flaw does not require any special PAN-OS configuration to be exploitable, making management-interface access restrictions an important immediate risk-reduction measure while updates are applied.
  • Although the vulnerability requires authentication, successful exploitation gives an attacker root-level control of the firewall, greatly increasing the potential impact of compromised management credentials.
  • Palo Alto Networks identified three U.S.-geolocated IP addresses assessed to be associated with exploit attempts, providing concrete indicators for organizations to review in their logs.
  • The available fixes vary by PAN-OS release branch, and PAN-OS 11.2.16 was listed with an October 15, 2026 estimated availability date, so organizations may need to select a branch-specific hotfix rather than wait for that release.
Key Points
  • 01Palo Alto Networks released security updates for CVE-2026-0322, a high-severity PAN-OS management-interface flaw with a CVSS score of 8.6 that is under active exploitation.
  • 02The flaw allows an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on affected firewalls.
  • 03Affected products include PAN-OS on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama virtual and M-Series systems, while Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected.
  • 04Palo Alto Networks said it has observed very limited exploitation and recommended restricting management-interface access to trusted internal IP addresses or a dedicated jump box.
  • 05CISA added CVE-2026-0322 and Cisco Secure Email Gateway flaw CVE-2026-76519 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Hackers exploit Collabora RCE flaw to backdoor Nextcloud servers
bleepingcomputer.com · 15 Oct 2026 20:25 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSbuilt-in-code-servercollabora-onlinecve-2026-110447githubnextcloudos-command-injectionphp-webshellrichdocumentscodesecond-security

In plain words

Hackers are using a serious weakness in an optional document-editing add-on for Nextcloud, a file-sharing service, to take control of affected servers without needing a password. The problem affects only Nextcloud installations using Collabora’s built-in CODE server, especially when that server is stopped after a restart, update, or crash; separate Collabora installations and Nextcloud All-in-One are not affected. Reported intruders placed hidden control files on servers and searched for password data and cryptocurrency wallets, so administrators need to install version 26.4.303 or later or remove the add-on. The case also shows how delays in publishing official vulnerability notices can leave organizations exposed while attackers move quickly.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-110447, a critical unauthenticated command-injection flaw in Nextcloud’s optional Collabora Online built-in CODE server app, to deploy PHP webshells and search for sensitive data. Administrators should upgrade richdocumentscode to version 26.4.303 or later or remove the app, since merely disabling it is insufficient.

Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-110447, a critical command-execution flaw in the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud versions before 26.4.303. Administrator reports indicate attacks began around September 10, before the formal advisory and CVE publication on October 14. Attackers send malicious requests to the app’s proxy.php endpoint to run operating-system commands without authentication or user interaction.

The issue affects only Nextcloud deployments using the optional built-in CODE server app, and exploitation requires that the bundled server be stopped, such as after a restart, upgrade, or crash. Administrators reported that attackers installed PHP webshells and searched servers for password databases, password-manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets; some also reported possible ransomware activity, though this was not independently confirmed. Collabora recommends upgrading to richdocumentscode 26.4.303 or later or removing the app if it is not needed, warning that disabling the app alone is insufficient.

The incident highlights a gap between the availability of security fixes and formal vulnerability notifications. Collabora committed a fix on September 9 and released version 26.4.303 on September 11, more than four weeks before the advisory and CVE were published. Second Security’s cited study found that public exploit code may appear within hours of a fix and before a CVE is issued, while the median delay between public fixes and CVE publication reached 39 days in August.

  • A system can become exploitable specifically when the built-in CODE server is not running after a restart, upgrade, or crash, rather than only while the service is operating normally.
  • Disabling the vulnerable Nextcloud app does not fully address the risk; Collabora advises upgrading it or removing it entirely if it is unnecessary.
  • The fix was committed on September 9 and released on September 11, but the advisory and CVE were not published until October 14, while administrators reported attacks beginning around September 10.
  • Second Security found that public exploit code can appear within hours of security fixes and before CVEs are published, making prompt application of available updates important even when formal vulnerability tracking information is absent.
Key Points
  • 01Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-110447, a critical command-execution flaw in Nextcloud’s Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) before version 26.4.303.
  • 02The attacks use a malicious request to the app’s proxy.php endpoint and can succeed without authentication or user interaction when the built-in CODE server is stopped, such as after a restart, upgrade, or crash.
  • 03The issue affects only the optional built-in CODE server app; standalone Collabora Online servers, Docker and RPM/DEB installations, and Nextcloud All-in-One deployments are not affected, according to Collabora.
  • 04Administrators reported that attackers installed PHP webshells and searched affected servers for password databases, password-manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets.
  • 05Collabora and Nextcloud recommend upgrading richdocumentscode to version 26.4.303 or later or removing the server app if it is not needed, because disabling the app alone is insufficient.

Langflow's Critical Authenticated RCE Flaw Targeted in 1,423 Honeypot Exploit Attempts
thehackernews.com · 15 Oct 2026 07:07 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSchinacommand-injectioncve-2026-105740datastaxenvironment-variable-injectionibmlangflowprevidianreverse-shellrussiaunited-states

In plain words

Attackers are trying to abuse a serious flaw in Langflow, a tool used to build AI applications, by logging in with ordinary user accounts and making the server run their commands. The issue affects Langflow versions older than 1.9.0, and researchers recorded more than 1,400 attempts against their test systems. If successful, attackers could take control of the server, steal secret settings and passwords, move into other connected systems, or leave a hidden way to return later. Organizations using Langflow should update it, turn off automatic login, and use strong, unique passwords.

Summary
Attackers are actively targeting the critical authenticated RCE flaw CVE-2026-105740 in Langflow, using weak or common credentials to run arbitrary commands through malicious MCP server configurations. Organizations should upgrade to Langflow 1.9.0 or later, disable auto-login, enforce strong credentials, and review MCP server API activity.

Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-105740, a critical Langflow flaw with a CVSS score of 9.9 that affects versions before 1.9.0. Langflow is an open-source platform for building AI applications and agentic workflows. Previdian recorded 1,423 exploitation attempts against its honeypot sensors from 27 attacker IP addresses since September 19, 2026, with activity increasing sharply on October 11.

The flaw lets any authenticated Langflow user, including a non-admin, create an MCP server configuration containing a command that is passed directly to the system shell without validation. Fetching the MCP server list triggers the stored command, which runs with the permissions of the Langflow process; the configuration can also execute again whenever that list is loaded. Captured attempts included commands to collect environment variables and Langflow secrets, access the host filesystem through Docker, and run basic system-identification commands. Langflow and Previdian recommend upgrading to a patched release, disabling auto-login, using strong unique passwords, avoiding direct exposure to untrusted networks, and reviewing authentication and MCP server API activity.

  • The flaw does not require administrator access: any authenticated Langflow account, including a regular user account, can run commands on the server.
  • A malicious MCP server configuration can remain stored and run again whenever the MCP server list is loaded, creating a persistent route back into the server.
  • These MCP server settings are stored in project settings rather than shown during normal flow-editor review, making malicious configurations easier to miss.
  • In one honeypot sequence, attackers failed to use disabled auto-login but then successfully logged in with a common username and password before immediately accessing the vulnerable endpoint.
  • Observed payloads sought Langflow secret keys and superuser passwords and attempted Docker-based access to the host filesystem, showing that attackers were pursuing more than simple command-execution testing.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-105740 is a critical authenticated remote code execution flaw affecting Langflow versions before 1.9.0.
  • 02An authenticated Langflow user can add an MCP server with a user-controlled command that Langflow passes to the system shell without validation.
  • 03Fetching the MCP server list can trigger the stored command, allowing it to run with the privileges of the Langflow process.
  • 04Previdian recorded 1,423 exploitation attempts against its honeypots from 27 attacker IP addresses beginning September 19, 2026.
  • 05Captured payloads attempted to collect Langflow secret settings and passwords, access the host filesystem through Docker commands, and run commands such as id and whoami.

Next.js Ships Out-of-Band Patch for Two Critical RCE Flaws in Caching and SVG Processing
thehackernews.com · 15 Oct 2026 12:28 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGScve-2026-96889ghsa-2464-fhr4-w9xwghsa-673q-mjm6-r5xrghsa-p3m5-59mp-jv5rlibrsvgnetlifynext-jsnext-ogreactreact-server-componentsserver-actionssharpuse-cachevercel
94
In plain words

Next.js issued an emergency update to fix two serious bugs that could let an outsider run commands on a website’s server, plus another bug that could overload a server and make a site unavailable. The highest risk is for sites using newer Next.js caching features, sites that process untrusted SVG image files on certain Linux servers, and apps that use server-side actions. Website owners should update to Next.js 16.4.1 or 15.5.28 and ensure the image-processing component Sharp is version 0.35.5 or newer, because attackers could otherwise take control of affected servers or disrupt services.

Summary
Next.js released emergency updates 16.4.1 and 15.5.28 to fix two critical unauthenticated RCE flaws in Cache Components and SVG processing, plus a high-severity Server Actions denial-of-service issue. Organizations should upgrade and, on Next.js 15, verify that sharp is updated to version 0.35.5 or later.

Next.js issued an out-of-band update on October 14, releasing versions 16.4.1 and 15.5.28 to fix two critical unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaws and a high-severity denial-of-service issue. One code-execution flaw affects Cache Components in Next.js 16 when a use cache function returns more than one typed array. The other affects SVG processing through the sharp package and librsvg on glibc-based Linux systems when attacker-supplied SVG files are processed. Vercel rated both code-execution issues 9.5 on the CVSS scale.

The Server Actions issue affects App Router applications with at least one Server Action and can force a server process to consume full CPU resources, preventing it from handling other requests. Organizations running Next.js 16 should upgrade to 16.4.1, while those running version 15 should upgrade to 15.5.28, rebuild, and redeploy. Next.js 15 users must also confirm that sharp is version 0.35.5 or later, because an existing affected 0.34.x version can remain installed after the framework upgrade. The Cache Components and Server Actions flaws have no workaround other than upgrading, while the SVG issue can temporarily be mitigated by updating or blocking SVG rendering in Sharp.

  • Upgrading to Next.js 15.5.28 alone may not remove the SVG risk because existing installations can retain affected Sharp 0.34.x versions; operators should verify Sharp with npm ls sharp and update it to 0.35.5 or later.
  • The SVG flaw is not exposed by default image optimization settings, but it can be reached when dangerouslyAllowSVG is enabled or when next/og generates social-preview images on the Node.js runtime.
  • The two Next.js 16 flaws involving use cache and Server Actions had no CVEs and were absent from npm audit’s advisory feed as of October 15, so automated dependency scans may not identify them.
  • For organizations unable to immediately update Next.js, Sharp can block SVG loading through sharp.block({ operation: ["VipsForeignLoadSvg"] }), but the Cache Components and Server Actions flaws have no workaround besides upgrading.
  • The image-related issue is the third Next.js code-execution problem tied to image processing since August, and this update resolves it by updating the bundled Sharp dependency rather than changing Next.js image-optimizer code.
Key Points
  • 01Next.js released out-of-band updates 16.4.1 and 15.5.28 on October 14 to address two critical remote-code-execution flaws and a high-severity denial-of-service flaw.
  • 02The Cache Components issue affects Next.js 16.0.0 through 16.4.0 when an App Router application enables Cache Components and a use cache function returns more than one typed array.
  • 03The SVG issue, CVE-2026-96889, can permit code execution when attacker-supplied SVG files reach Sharp on glibc-based Linux, and it is fixed by Sharp 0.35.5 or later.
  • 04The Server Actions denial-of-service issue affects App Router applications with at least one Server Action and can cause a server process to use all available CPU resources.
  • 05Organizations should upgrade, rebuild, and redeploy; Next.js 15 users should also check npm ls sharp because upgrading Next.js may leave an affected Sharp 0.34.x version installed.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a critical out-of-band patch for widely used Next.js releases, addressing two unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaws and a high-severity denial-of-service issue. Security professionals responsible for affected applications should promptly upgrade, rebuild, redeploy, and verify the installed Sharp version on Next.js 15.

In plain words

Ahsay Backup released new updates for its AhsayCBS backup software after earlier updates did not fully fix two security weaknesses. Criminals have been using the weaknesses to get into exposed systems without permission, place hidden remote-control tools, and run software that mines cryptocurrency. Organizations using affected AhsayCBS versions should install the new fixes and restart their servers, because compromised backup systems could put customer data at risk.

Summary
Ahsay Backup released new AhsayCBS hotfixes after earlier patches failed to fully fix two actively exploited flaws that enable unauthenticated remote code execution. Organizations should update to v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70 and reboot servers to prevent web-shell and XMRig miner deployments.

Ahsay Backup released new hotfixes for two actively exploited AhsayCBS security flaws, CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134. The flaws can be chained to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Huntress observed threat actors using them against exposed systems to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners.

Ahsay said that earlier releases, AhsayCBS 9.15.2.59 and 10.3.4.0, did not completely fix the issues. The updated fixes are AhsayCBS v10.3.4.45 and v9.15.2.70 hotfixes, and Ahsay instructed customers to reboot their servers after installation. Huntress independently verified that the v10.3.4.45 hotfix mitigates the initial entry point used in the observed attack chain.

CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog because of active exploitation. U.S. federal agencies are required to apply the patches by October 17, 2026. Ahsay urged customers to act immediately to protect their environments and customer data.

  • Organizations that installed the August 2026 AhsayCBS updates may still be exposed, because Ahsay confirmed those earlier patches did not completely resolve the flaws.
  • Huntress independently verified that the v10.3.4.45 hotfix blocks the initial entry point used in the observed attack chain, which remained possible on previous v10 releases.
  • The affected software is a backup platform, so Ahsay specifically warned that delayed remediation could endanger customers' data.
  • CISA's addition of both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog requires U.S. federal agencies to apply the patches by October 17, 2026.

  • 05The new fixes are AhsayCBS v10.3.4.45 and v9.15.2.70 hotfixes, and CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

In plain words

A campaign called GhostAction took over about 1,900 GitHub user accounts and used them to place harmful automated instructions in more than 30,000 software projects. These instructions tried to collect passwords and access keys used by developers, including keys for cloud services, software package sites, and AI services. This matters because stolen keys can let criminals access or misuse the services and software connected to affected projects, especially where old keys were never changed.

Summary
GhostAction attackers compromised roughly 1,900 GitHub accounts to push malicious GitHub Actions workflows into more than 30,000 repositories and steal CI/CD secrets. GitHub began blocking the workflow on October 9, limiting later waves, but previously exposed or unrotated credentials remain at risk.

GhostAction, a GitHub-focused supply chain campaign, targeted more than 30,000 repositories across 3,000 users and organizations in activity observed on October 8 and 9, 2026. GitGuardian said attackers compromised about 1,900 GitHub accounts and attempted to extract 3,174 secrets from public repositories’ continuous-integration environments. The campaign is intended to steal CI/CD secrets, cloud credentials, package-registry tokens, and AI-provider API keys.

The attackers obtained repository write access using stolen Personal Access Tokens or credentials from infostealer logs and dumps, then added malicious GitHub Actions workflow files with deceptive names. Newer payloads scanned Git history for secrets, including AWS key IDs, and later versions collected nearby context to match key IDs with their secret access keys. GitHub began preventing the malicious workflow from running on October 9, blocking secret extraction in later waves observed on October 10 and 12, although some affected victims had also been compromised in earlier waves.

  • The attackers used a phased rollout, first deploying the payload to 160 previously observed victims and then expanding to 28,000 new repositories only 20 minutes later.
  • Later payload versions captured nearby text around AWS key IDs, enabling the attackers to associate an exposed key ID with its corresponding secret access key.
  • Some repositories affected in the 2026 burst had also been compromised in 2025 and earlier in 2026, indicating that previously exposed secrets may not have been rotated.
  • GitHub's prevention of the malicious workflow beginning October 9 stopped the October 10 and 12 waves from extracting secrets despite those waves using the same payload.
Key Points
  • 01GhostAction targeted more than 30,000 GitHub repositories across 3,000 users and organizations during a spike observed on October 8 and 9, 2026.
  • 02The campaign compromised about 1,900 GitHub accounts and attempted to extract 3,174 secrets from public repositories' continuous-integration environments.
  • 03Attackers used stolen Personal Access Tokens or credentials from infostealer logs and dumps to gain repository write access and add malicious GitHub Actions workflow files.
  • 04The malicious workflows sought CI/CD secrets, cloud credentials, package-registry tokens, and AI-provider API keys, and later variants scanned Git history for secrets including AWS key IDs.
  • 05GitHub began preventing the malicious workflow from running on October 9, so subsequent waves observed on October 10 and 12 could not extract secrets.

This is a high-impact active supply-chain campaign that compromised about 1,900 GitHub accounts and targeted more than 30,000 repositories for CI/CD, cloud, package-registry, and AI-service credentials.     Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers target governments across former Soviet states
    therecord.media · 15 Oct 2026 13:55 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra

    In plain words

    Researchers say a group believed to have links to Kazakhstan has tried to break into government offices in Central Asia and other former Soviet countries, including Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. It used convincing emails with harmful files, sometimes sent from government email accounts it had already taken over, and in one case used a flaw in WinRAR, a file-compression program. The targets handle foreign relations, economic planning, energy, water and environmental issues, so stolen information could affect diplomatic talks, resource decisions and regional security.

    Summary
    Researchers say a suspected Kazakhstan-linked espionage group has targeted government agencies across former Soviet states for diplomatic, economic, energy and water-resource intelligence. The group uses phishing, compromised government email accounts, GitHub-hosted payloads, and recently exploited the WinRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088 against a likely Armenian foreign ministry target.

    Cisco Talos and Recorded Future’s Insikt Group said a suspected Kazakhstan-linked cyber-espionage group, tracked as UAT-6275 and TAG-193, has run at least eight campaigns since January 2025. The group targeted or showed interest in government institutions across nine countries, including Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Its targets include agencies handling foreign affairs, economic development, agriculture, environmental management, energy supplies and water resources.

    Researchers assessed with medium confidence that the group has ties to Kazakhstan, based on Russian-language malware material, testing activity from Kazakhstan, working-hour patterns, and overlap with earlier YoroTrooper operations. The attackers commonly sent phishing emails with malicious attachments, sometimes from already-compromised government email accounts, and used GitHub to store malicious scripts and files. In April 2026, the group was observed exploiting the WinRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088 in an operation likely targeting Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, its first observed use of a software vulnerability to deliver malware.

    • The group’s activity was timed near diplomatic developments, including a Tajik target after treaty discussions with Kazakhstan and a Belarusian target before a bilateral meeting, which researchers said could indicate interest in diplomatic developments.
    • Information held by agencies managing water, energy and transport has particular strategic value in Central Asia because river systems and infrastructure are interconnected across the region.
    • The use of previously compromised government email accounts can make malicious messages appear more credible than messages sent from unfamiliar addresses.
    • The April 2026 WinRAR operation was the first observed case of the group using a software flaw to deliver harmful software, marking an expansion beyond deceptive emails and documents.
    Key Points

In plain words

A group known as Silent Lynx has targeted government organizations in Central Asia and other former Soviet states by sending convincing emails with official-looking documents. Opening these files can give the attackers remote control of a victim’s computer, including through a flaw in the WinRAR file-compression program. The targets include agencies connected to diplomacy, economic affairs, environmental work, and energy, putting sensitive government information and regional resource management at risk.

Summary
Silent Lynx, a Kazakhstan-linked threat actor, targeted CIS government organizations with spear-phishing campaigns that delivered custom reverse shells through macros, PowerShell downloaders, malicious archives, and a WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 exploit. Its adoption of vulnerability exploitation and persistence mechanisms indicates an expanding regional espionage capability.

Silent Lynx, also tracked as UAT-6275 and TAG-193, targeted government organizations across Central Asia and the wider Commonwealth of Independent States from June 2025 through August 2026. Observed victims and lure themes spanned Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus. The campaign used diplomatic, trade, energy, and aviation-themed emails, including messages sent from compromised government accounts. Its targets included agencies tied to diplomacy, economic affairs, environmental work, and energy infrastructure.

The group used four delivery paths: macro-enabled Word documents, PS2EXE-packaged PowerShell downloaders, malicious shortcuts inside RAR archives, and RAR archives exploiting the WinRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088. These chains delivered custom reverse shells named FoalShell, Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell, which provide interactive remote access to compromised systems. Later activity used scheduled tasks and the Windows Startup folder to make payloads run automatically after user logon. The April 2026 WinRAR chain was the first documented instance of UAT-6275 weaponizing a security flaw for malware delivery.

Publicly accessible staging directories linked to the threat actor also hosted Linux-compatible tools and a proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2025-25257, an SQL injection flaw in Fortinet FortiWeb. Cisco Talos said the group’s continued activity and adoption of new delivery techniques suggest it will continue seeking access to government organizations in Central Asia and the CIS. The article links Silent Lynx to a Kazakhstan-nexus activity cluster with assessed overlaps involving YoroTrooper, ShadowSilk, Cavalry Werewolf, and Tomiris.

  • Silent Lynx shifted from document- and downloader-based delivery to exploiting CVE-2025-8088 in April 2026, its first documented use of a security flaw to deliver malware.
  • The group used compromised government email accounts and official-looking documents, increasing the apparent credibility of phishing messages sent to government targets.
  • Later attack chains placed PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder, allowing it to launch automatically when a user logs in.
  • Public staging directories linked to the group contained Linux-compatible tools and a proof-of-concept for Fortinet FortiWeb CVE-2025-25257, indicating that its available tooling extended beyond the observed Windows-focused infection chains.
Key Points

    Summary
    Confiant found that Discover-Tech allegedly weaponized programmatic advertising to build a global identity graph, siphon first-party cookies, fingerprint devices, and selectively deliver encrypted remote code through infrastructure linked by Citizen Lab to Candiru spyware.     Confiant reported that Discover-Tech (DTech) used advertising infrastructure to collect extensive device, network, behavioral, and identity data from web users. Confiant also identified connections between Discover-Tech, MyIPInfo, Akedo, Adtimizer, Tekma, and Intelos, which it describes as an ADINT-focused cyber-surveillance company.

In plain words

Researchers say an Israeli spyware maker, Candiru, used ordinary online ads to secretly infect devices at Al Jazeera without users clicking anything. The ads first checked whether a phone or computer belonged to a chosen target, then sent harmful software only to those devices; at least 45 Al Jazeera devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025. This matters because the same ad system reached tens of thousands of apps and websites, showing that everyday advertising can be used as a hidden route for government-linked surveillance of journalists and others.

Summary
Citizen Lab found that Israeli spyware vendor Candiru targeted at least 45 Al Jazeera devices through zero-click online ads placed by Discover-Tech, using advertising identifiers to selectively deliver exploits. Major ad platforms removed or blocked Discover-Tech after the findings, highlighting how ad-tech infrastructure can be weaponized for covert surveillance.

Citizen Lab reported that Candiru spyware was delivered to Al Jazeera devices through ordinary online advertisements, with no click or other action required from users. At least 45 Al Jazeera devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025, and researchers linked the activity to Candiru with high confidence. The researchers recovered a Windows spyware file from one compromised device, but did not recover the code used for the initial browser or app break-in.

The advertisements, placed by Israeli ad company Discover-Tech, sent a device’s advertising ID and internet address to a server that decided whether it belonged to a target. Targeted devices received attack code, while other devices received nothing, leaving ad networks little malicious content in the ads themselves to detect. Citizen Lab said this was the first public technical confirmation of mercenary spyware reaching real devices through targeted advertising, and Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi took action against Discover-Tech after the findings were shared.

Discover-Tech’s ad code appeared in about 75,000 phone apps and 120,000 websites, while Confiant estimated its traffic at roughly 10 million ads per day. The ads were observed on networks belonging to governments, large institutions, news organizations, and technology companies, although an ad’s appearance on a network does not prove infection. Citizen Lab and Confiant published domains, files, and connection indicators so organizations can block them or look for a sequence involving a Discover-Tech server, a Candiru screening server, and a command-and-control server.

  • The ad networks could not readily detect the operation because the advertisements themselves contained no harmful code; the Discover-Tech server decided separately whether to send attack code after receiving device information.
  • Citizen Lab described this as the first public technical confirmation that government-sold spyware reached real devices through targeted online advertisements, although the browser or app break-in code was not recovered.
  • Organizations can search for a distinctive three-step connection pattern in their records: a Discover-Tech ad server, followed by a Candiru screening server, then a spyware control server.
  • Discover-Tech advertisements appeared across roughly 75,000 mobile apps and 120,000 websites, but their presence on an organization’s network alone does not show that a device there was infected.
  • The Candiru-linked ads identified by Confiant were low-volume and mostly reached home and mobile internet connections rather than the sensitive institutional networks where the broader advertising traffic was seen.
Key Points
  • 01Citizen Lab reported that Candiru spyware infections at Al Jazeera were delivered through online advertisements that ran code as soon as an ad loaded, without requiring a user click.
  • 02Discover-Tech advertisements sent a device's advertising ID and internet address to a server, which returned attack code only when it identified the device as a target.
  • 03Citizen Lab said at least 45 Al Jazeera devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025 and linked the operation to Candiru with high confidence.

  • 05After Citizen Lab shared its findings, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi removed, blocked, paused, or suspended Discover-Tech's advertising access.

In plain words

Researchers found a serious flaw in the Linux software that helps run many cloud computers, allowing a program inside an isolated virtual computer to read information from the larger physical computer hosting it. The flaw was demonstrated in Vercel’s live cloud sandboxes, though there is no report that customer files, secrets, or application data were read and no known real-world abuse. It matters because many cloud providers rely on the same kind of separation between customers, so an attacker who already gets code running in one virtual computer could potentially affect the host and other services on it. Providers need to update the host computer’s Linux software and restart it; updating only the isolated virtual computer is not enough.

Summary
A critical Linux kernel networking flaw dubbed PwnEscape (CVE-2026-99999) can let code in a guest VM leak host memory and potentially crash or compromise the host, threatening cloud sandbox isolation. Cloud operators should patch and reboot host kernels to vendor-fixed builds; updating guest kernels alone does not address the issue.

A critical Linux kernel networking flaw called PwnEscape, tracked as CVE-2026-99999, can allow code running inside a virtual machine to read memory from its host computer. Researcher Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai demonstrated the memory leak against Vercel’s production cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed the result. The article reports no known real-world exploitation and no evidence that customer files, secrets, or application data were accessed.

The researcher said each crafted packet could return about 32 bytes of host memory and that the process could continue while packets were sent. In lab systems configured to match Vercel’s environment, the same flaw was also used to crash a host with two packets and to reach administrator control, though the researcher did not claim production root-code execution. Linux maintainers released and backported a fix, but its author described it as defense in depth; operators should update and reboot host kernels, since updating only guest virtual machines does not address the issue.

  • The memory disclosure could be repeated indefinitely as long as the guest continued sending crafted packets, despite each packet returning only about 32 bytes of host memory.
  • Two specially crafted packets were sufficient to crash a lab host configured like Vercel’s environment, taking down every sandbox running on that host.
  • The published kernel change is described by its author as a defense-in-depth measure rather than a complete solution, with fuller validation of incoming packets still needed.
  • pwn.ai said it found the flaw in three days using an AI-assisted research system for under $700 in API-token costs, while researchers directed and validated the work.
Key Points
  • 01PwnEscape, tracked as CVE-2026-99999, is a critical Linux kernel networking flaw that can allow code running inside a virtual machine to read memory from its host computer.
  • 02A researcher demonstrated the host-memory leak against Vercel’s production sandboxes, with each outbound packet able to return about 32 bytes of host memory.
  • 03On lab systems configured to match Vercel’s environment, the researcher also used the flaw to crash a host with two crafted packets and reached administrator control of a host.
  • 04The flaw requires an attacker to already be able to run code inside a guest virtual machine, and the article reports no known real-world exploitation or evidence that customer files, secrets, or application data were accessed.
  • 05Linux maintainers backported a fix to supported stable branches, and cloud operators should update and reboot the host kernel because updating only guest kernels does not resolve the issue.

In plain words

Drupal fixed a serious flaw that could let someone run commands on a website’s server, potentially without needing to log in when certain add-on modules are installed. The problem affects sites using supported Drupal versions unless they install the new updates; older, no-longer-supported versions have no official fix. Website owners should update promptly or temporarily remove the Field UI feature, because public attack code or real-world attacks could appear soon after the fix becomes known.

Summary
Drupal released critical security updates for a Field UI remote code execution flaw (CVE-2026-108097) that can be reachable through contributed modules, including at least one no-login path. Sites should immediately update to fixed Drupal versions or temporarily uninstall Field UI if updates are not possible.

Drupal released updates on October 14 for CVE-2026-108097, a critical remote code execution flaw in the Field UI core module. The issue is fixed in Drupal 11.4.10, 11.3.19, and 10.6.19, while end-of-life branches including Drupal 11.2.x and below, 10.5.x and below, Drupal 8, and Drupal 9 have no fix. Drupal said core alone does not expose the flaw, but contributed modules or custom code can create exploit paths, including at least one known path requiring no login.

The flaw stemmed from Field UI running a PHP callback specified in a table row’s #region_callback value without checking which callback it was. The fix removes that callback execution and instead obtains each row’s region directly from row and table values. Sites unable to update can temporarily uninstall the field_ui module, although this disables administrative pages for managing fields and display settings. A separate critical issue in the Entity List contributed module, CVE-2026-108099, has similar conditions and requires its own update, while the same Drupal core releases also address two logged-in-user cross-site scripting issues in the Link and Navigation modules.

  • The vulnerable behavior had existed in Field UI since at least Drupal 8.9.0, even though Drupal’s general rendering system had blocked untrusted callbacks since 2019.
  • Updating Drupal core alone does not fix the separately affected Entity List module; sites using that module must update it independently to version 3.0.10.
  • Uninstalling Field UI is a temporary protective measure, but it prevents administrators from using the pages that manage fields and their display settings.
  • In the reported usage data, 151,442 of 531,499 Drupal sites were on affected branches that received no fix because those branches were end-of-life.

  • 04The Entity List contributed module has a separate critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-108099, and requires its own update because updating Drupal core does not update the module.
  • 05The same Drupal core releases also address two moderately critical cross-site scripting flaws in the Link and Navigation modules.

A cyberattack on BAE Systems disrupted the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC), the platform that produces and sends bankruptcy notices for all U.S. federal bankruptcy courts. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts said all access to BNC systems and related websites operated by BAE was unavailable. Production of bankruptcy notices was halted as a result.

The disruption follows other recent cyber incidents affecting U.S. court systems, including a breach of Arizona’s state court system and earlier attacks on federal court case-filing and docketing systems.

In plain words

Researchers found a campaign targeting government organizations and government-linked systems that run Linux, a common computer operating system. The attackers used AI-assisted code and hidden access tools to steal passwords, search government email accounts and databases, and try to send sensitive information out of the victims’ networks. This matters because access to official email, social-media accounts, and government data could enable espionage, impersonation, and further compromise, while the attackers also tried to erase evidence of their activity.

Summary
Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 tracked CL-UNK-1211, an espionage campaign targeting government and state-affiliated Linux infrastructure that used AI-assisted scripts, web shells, credential theft, SysGoRAT, reverse shells, and data-exfiltration tools. The campaign combined persistent access and anti-forensic cleanup with attempts to steal government mailboxes and database data.

Unit 42 identified CL-UNK-1211, an espionage campaign observed from October 2025 through April 2026 that targeted government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, particularly Linux systems. The attackers sought persistent access, performed extensive reconnaissance, and attempted to obtain sensitive database contents and government mailboxes. Unit 42 reported that the activity included attempts to use official government email accounts to facilitate access to social-media accounts. The cluster has not been attributed to a specific nation-state or cybercrime group.

The campaign used web shells, custom and open-source tools, in-memory remote shells, SSH access, proxy utilities, and a custom cross-platform Go remote-access Trojan called SysGoRAT. Attackers established persistence by modifying PHP configuration files so a malicious script would execute before other PHP scripts, and they also harvested passwords through a modified .bashrc file that imitated the sudo password prompt. Several payloads contained conversational comments and developer-reasoning notes that Unit 42 said were consistent with AI-assisted generation or automated AI-agent execution. The attackers also used scripts and commands to search for cleartext credentials, scan networks and databases, move between systems, and prepare data for exfiltration.

The operators attempted to evade investigation by trying to terminate Cortex XDR-related processes, deleting logs and temporary files, changing file timestamps, and planting red-team-themed markers such as RedTeamOps2025 and pentest123. Unit 42 stated that Cortex XDR detected and mitigated attempts to suppress endpoint protections, and that protections were not disabled. The report provides file hashes, IP addresses, and domains associated with the activity, along with descriptions of the observed techniques. Palo Alto Networks said its Advanced WildFire, URL and DNS protections, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, and Cortex Cloud are designed to help detect or prevent threats discussed in the report.

  • The attackers used PHP’s auto_prepend_file setting across standard and Plesk PHP configuration directories, causing their malicious script to run before other PHP scripts and making the web shell persist broadly on affected servers.
  • A modified .bashrc file impersonated the sudo password prompt, recorded users’ passwords in a file named Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt, and then passed the password to the legitimate sudo command so the interception would be less noticeable.
  • The mailbox-search script was aimed at finding social-media-related messages in government email accounts, indicating that official mailboxes were used as a route toward access to associated external accounts.
  • Some attacker-generated scripts contained syntax errors that would prevent them from running, including a mailbox-compression script with a broken variable assignment.
  • The attackers planted markers such as RedTeamOps2025 and a user password of pentest123 to make malicious activity appear to be an authorized security assessment during later investigation.
Key Points

  • 05The attackers attempted to harvest credentials, access government mailboxes and databases, exfiltrate data, disable endpoint protections, delete logs, alter file timestamps, and disguise some activity as red-team work.

In plain words

NGINX released updates to fix five security problems in its widely used web-server software, including flaws that could crash websites, possibly let an outsider run code on a server, or in rare cases get around website client-certificate checks. The issues affect organizations running certain NGINX features, such as newer HTTP/3 connections, shared login-session storage, or particular website routing and page-inclusion settings. Organizations should install NGINX 1.30.6 or 1.31.7, because older versions may remain exposed unless their operating-system provider has included the fixes.

Summary
NGINX released 1.30.6 and 1.31.7 to patch five flaws, including three potentially code-execution-capable memory bugs and a TLS session-ticket issue that could bypass client-certificate verification. Organizations should upgrade promptly or apply configuration-specific mitigations, particularly where shared TLS session caches, HTTP/3, AIO/SSI, regex maps, or alias rewrites are enabled.

NGINX released versions 1.30.6 and 1.31.7 on October 14 to fix five medium-rated security flaws. Three are memory bugs that can crash worker processes and could possibly allow code execution in specific configurations. The issues are not reported as exploited, and none was listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 15. F5 assigned CVSS v4.0 scores of 9.2 to the three memory issues, 8.3 to the TLS issue, and 6.9 to the HTTP/3 issue.

The flaws require particular NGINX settings, including alias with URI rewrites, regex maps, AIO with SSI pages, HTTP/3, or a shared TLS session cache. The TLS flaw, CVE-2026-97629, can allow a forged session that could bypass client-certificate checks when automatic session-ticket key rotation is used; F5 says this occurs non-deterministically and is beyond an attacker’s control. The HTTP/3 flaw, CVE-2026-95101, can send extra bytes to a backend or allow a request body beyond the configured size limit when proxy request buffering is enabled. Other issues involve heap overflows or a use-after-free condition in worker processes.

NGINX recommends upgrading to stable version 1.30.6 or mainline version 1.31.7, while F5 provides configuration-specific workarounds for organizations unable to update immediately. NGINX only publishes fixes for those two branches, so users of older branches must verify whether their distribution has backported the patches. Administrators can use nginx -T to review the active configuration for the affected feature combinations.

  • All five issues require particular NGINX configuration directives, so exposure depends on enabled features rather than affecting every default installation in the same way.
  • The TLS issue can affect deployments using NGINX’s own documented shared-session-cache example when automatic ticket-key rotation is enabled without manually supplied keys.
  • The HTTP/3 issue is especially actionable because proxy request buffering is enabled by default, allowing extra request data to reach a backend or pass beyond the configured body-size limit under the affected conditions.
  • NGINX publishes fixes only for its 1.30 and 1.31 branches, so users of older branches must confirm that their operating-system or distribution vendor has backported the patches.
  • Administrators can identify relevant exposure paths by running "nginx -T" and checking for the specific combinations of alias and rewrite, regex maps, AIO with SSI, HTTP/3 listeners, and shared TLS session caches described in the article.
Key Points
  • 01NGINX released versions 1.30.6 and 1.31.7 on October 14 to address five vulnerabilities affecting specific configurations.
  • 02Three of the vulnerabilities are memory-safety bugs that can crash NGINX worker processes and may allow code execution under the required configurations.
  • 03CVE-2026-97629 can enable a forged TLS session that could bypass client-certificate verification when a shared TLS session cache uses automatically rotated ticket keys.
  • 04CVE-2026-95101 affects HTTP/3 deployments with proxy request buffering enabled and can cause extra bytes to be sent to a backend or bypass the configured request-body-size limit.
  • 05NGINX recommends upgrading to 1.30.6 or 1.31.7, while F5 provides configuration-specific workarounds for organizations that cannot upgrade immediately.

    In plain words

    Researchers linked a long-running online scam operation called Help TDS to Hotejka, which is believed to be a new name for an older group called ROI777. The operation sends people from hacked websites, spam, and other online links to fake Microsoft warning screens that pressure them to call a support number. Call-center staff then try to persuade victims to install software that gives them full control of the victim’s computer, allowing repeat fraud. The group has used more than 20,000 free Cloudflare Pages sites since April 2026, showing how cheaply and quickly scammers can build large-scale infrastructure.

    Summary
    Infoblox linked the long-running Help TDS traffic-distribution system to Hotejka, likely a rebrand of ROI777, which routes traffic from compromised sites to tech-support scams that seek remote access to victims' devices. Since April 2026, the operation has reportedly created more than 20,000 Cloudflare Pages domains to host disposable scam infrastructure.

    Infoblox linked the long-running Help TDS traffic-distribution system to Hotejka, a Russian-language affiliate program believed to be a rebrand of ROI777. Active since at least 2017, Help TDS sends visitors from compromised websites and other sources to tech-support scams that display fake Windows security alerts. Victims are urged to call a supposed Microsoft support number, where call-center operators may persuade them to install remote desktop software such as Ultraviewer. This can give the operators complete control of the victim’s computer and enable repeated fraud.

    Help TDS uses specially crafted affiliate links and evaluates visitors using browser fingerprinting, location, device details, IP reputation, and checks for automated browsers before choosing a destination. It can route users to fake support pages or pass their traffic to another affiliate platform, where it may be evaluated and resold again; some paths lead to fake CAPTCHA pages that enroll browsers for push-notification spam. Since April 2026, the operators have used free Cloudflare Pages sites, creating about 300 disposable pages each day, with more than 20,000 such domains detected. Infoblox said roughly 20 affiliates, including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay, send traffic into Help TDS, and assessed that Hotejka/ROI777 may have earned at least several million dollars through affiliate platforms over eight years.

    • The operation does not send every visitor to the same destination: it checks browser and location details before deciding whether to show a tech-support scam or pass the visitor to another advertising platform for resale.
    • The fraud is designed to create ongoing access rather than only obtain a payment, because callers may be persuaded to install remote-control software that lets operators return to the computer later.
    • Historical command-and-control domains, affiliate-platform use, and traffic-tracking identifiers provided Infoblox with multiple independent links between Hotejka and the earlier ROI777 operation.
    • The use of roughly 300 disposable Cloudflare Pages sites per day illustrates how the operation can rapidly replace scam pages as individual domains are detected or removed.
    • Help TDS functions as shared routing infrastructure for numerous affiliates, including website-compromise operations, rather than being limited to a single source of malicious traffic.

In plain words

The article links a long-running online scam network called Help TDS to a Russian-language group known as Hotejka. The group sends people from hacked websites, ads, social-media posts, and spam to frightening fake Microsoft warning pages that urge them to call a number; callers are then pressured to install software that gives scammers control of their computer. This can affect individuals and organizations, because the scammers may gain repeated access to files and systems and use it for theft or extortion. Researchers found a way to spot many of the group’s new scam websites before they are used, helping reduce exposure.

Summary
Infoblox attributes the long-running Help TDS tech-support-scam operation to the Russian-language Hotejka affiliate program, likely a rebrand of ROI777, which funnels victims to call centers that attempt to install UltraViewer remote-access software. The researchers developed detections that predict Hotejka’s rapidly created Cloudflare Pages domains about seven days before use, substantially reducing customer exposure.

Infoblox assesses that the Russian-language Hotejka affiliate program operates Help TDS, a long-running traffic-routing system that delivers tech-support scams, and that Hotejka is likely a rebrand of ROI777. Affiliates send users from compromised websites, malvertising, social-media posts, spam, and other sources into the system, which evaluates visitors and sends selected victims to fake Microsoft browser-lock pages. The pages use alarming messages, sounds, and a supposed Microsoft Security phone number to persuade users to contact a call center, where operators attempt to have them install UltraViewer remote-access software.

Since April 2026, Hotejka has used large numbers of free Cloudflare Pages subdomains for Help TDS, creating roughly 300 new domains daily while more than 125,000 new pages.dev subdomains appear across the service each day. Infoblox reverse engineered the operator’s naming patterns and reported detecting likely Hotejka domains about seven days before they were used, identifying more than 16,000 domains later used for the TDS through mid-September. The company said observed exposure among its cloud customers fell from as much as 4% on a single day to around 0.5% after the detections were deployed.

  • Hotejka’s affiliate code retrieves the current scam domain from a Telegram channel or a fallback JSON source, caches it locally, and refreshes it every 30 seconds, allowing affiliates to rotate destinations without changing their embedded code.
  • The affiliate lures are limited to U.S. business hours, calculated using Moscow time, so victims are sent to the call center only when operators are expected to be available.
  • Although Hotejka announces about 300 Cloudflare Pages domains per day for Help TDS, Infoblox detected roughly 30,000 likely related domains in six months and found that only about 16,000 were announced, indicating the use of additional pages beyond those publicly listed as TDS infrastructure.
  • Some Help TDS Cloudflare Pages domains display harmless-looking decoy content when visited directly, including fake financial-application advertisements and a Ledger impersonation, before later appearing in the operator’s C2-domain announcements.
  • The operation also uses DNS CNAME records to route affiliate-owned domains to Hotejka-controlled infrastructure, allowing a visitor to be redirected through DNS rather than through the main Help TDS path.
Key Points
  • 01Infoblox assesses that the Russian-language Hotejka affiliate program operates Help TDS and that Hotejka is likely a rebrand of ROI777, which was exposed for similar activity in 2018.
  • 02Help TDS directs victims from compromised websites, malvertising, social-media posts, and spam to fake Microsoft browser-lock pages that display a phone number for a purported technical-support service.
  • 03During a call-center interaction, an operator identifying himself as Microsoft Technical Support directed researchers to download UltraViewer, a remote desktop tool that would provide the attacker full access to the system.
  • 04Since April 2026, the operators have used free Cloudflare Pages sites and announced nearly 300 new domains daily through a Telegram channel, with each domain resolving for about one week.
  • 05Infoblox reported that its detection algorithms identified likely Hotejka Cloudflare Pages domains an average of seven days before their use and reduced observed customer exposure from as much as 4% on a day to around 0.5%.

    In plain words

    The UK Legal Aid Agency says criminals broke into its computer systems in April 2025 and took records that may date back as far as 1978. The stolen information can include personal and financial details of people who applied for or received legal aid, as well as information about law firms and other organizations that provide it. This matters because such details could cause serious privacy and financial risks, and it highlights the need to improve the security of public services that handle sensitive information.

    Summary
    The UK Legal Aid Agency says an April 2025 cyberattack exposed data spanning back to 1978, including roughly 250,000 records from before 2007. The agency says it has no evidence the stolen personal data has been published and is accelerating modernization of its digital systems.

    The UK Legal Aid Agency (LAA) said attackers who breached its IT systems in April 2025 stole records dating as far back as 1978. The agency initially disclosed the incident in early May, warning that legal-aid provider payment information might have been compromised. It later confirmed that the breach was more serious, involving a large amount of sensitive data from legal-aid applicants and recipients.

    Most of the affected data concerns applications, claims, payments, or live cases from January 2007 through 16 May 2025, but the LAA identified approximately 250,000 records from before 2007. Stolen information includes contact details, dates of birth, national ID numbers, criminal history, employment status, contribution amounts, debts, and payments, while provider data included contracts, financial details, and LAA Online Portal credentials. The Ministry of Justice said it has no evidence that the data has been published and stated that it is investing more than £200 million to modernize legal-aid digital services, improve resilience, and strengthen security.

    • The confirmed scope expanded substantially after the initial May 2025 disclosure, which had warned primarily that legal-aid provider payment information might have been compromised.
    • Although most affected records are from 2007 onward, the agency identified approximately 250,000 records from before 2007, with the earliest verified record dating to 1978.
    • The incident affects both people seeking legal aid and the organizations delivering it, because provider portal credentials, contracts, financial information, and contact details were also taken.
    • The Ministry of Justice had already committed £20 million to stabilize and upgrade the agency’s digital systems before the incident and now says it is investing more than £200 million in modernization and security improvements.

    • 01The UK Legal Aid Agency said attackers who breached its IT systems in April 2025 stole records dating as far back as 1978.

    • 03Stolen information includes sensitive applicant and recipient details, such as contact information, dates of birth, national ID numbers, criminal history, employment status, contribution amounts, debts, and payments.

Britain’s Legal Aid Agency (LAA) said further investigation has found that a cyberattack exposed a broader and older collection of personal records than first reported. Criminals exploited weaknesses in the LAA’s IT systems, accessed systems containing personal information, and copied some of that data. While the breach was initially described as affecting users of its online legal-aid service since 2010, officials now say about 250,000 records predate 2007, with the earliest verified record dating from 1978.

The stolen material can vary by case and may include names, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, financial information, bank and property details, legal-aid case information, and partially redacted payment card details. The LAA said the full impact is difficult to assess because much of the data is unstructured, fragmented, or incomplete, while the Ministry of Justice says it has no indication the material has been published or shared. The ministry has strengthened access controls and monitoring and is retiring or isolating higher-risk legacy systems.

In plain words

India has told phone companies to show the registered name of a caller alongside the phone number for incoming calls on 4G and newer networks from November 1, 2026. This will affect mobile phone users and telecom providers in India, making it easier for people to recognize calls from numbers they have not saved. The change is intended to help people spot spam and scam calls, while allowing callers to hide their identity if they choose and letting eligible businesses use a verified business name.

Summary
India will require telecom providers to display the subscriber-registered name of domestic callers on 4G and newer networks starting November 1, 2026, aiming to make unknown and fraudulent calls easier to identify.

India has directed telecom service providers to display a caller’s registered name alongside their phone number for incoming calls on 4G and newer networks starting November 1, 2026. The Department of Telecommunications issued the requirement for Calling Name Presentation (CNAP), which is intended to help users identify unknown callers and address spam or fraudulent calls. The initial rollout does not cover 2G, 3G, or traditional landline networks; those networks will be considered separately.

A recipient will continue to see the phone number first, followed by either the name saved in their own contacts or, for an unsaved domestic number, the name held in the originating provider’s subscriber records. Calls from outside India will show the label “International Call.” Providers must maintain subscriber-name databases, support queries between originating and receiving networks, avoid retaining caller-name information after a call ends, and offer callers an option to hide their identity. Business and bulk-connection users may use a preferred name only when it is supported by a registered trademark or a trade name registered on the Goods and Services Tax portal.

  • The displayed name for an unsaved domestic number will come from the originating telecom provider's subscriber records, rather than from a name chosen by the receiving phone user.
  • Telecom providers must ensure that caller-name information is not retained after the incoming call ends.
  • The system requires the provider receiving a call to query the originating provider's subscriber-name database, creating a need for supporting database, network, and connectivity infrastructure.
  • Businesses and bulk-connection users can replace their registered caller name only with a trademark or GST-registered trade name, with supporting documents required for new connections.
  • Calls originating outside India will be labeled "International Call" instead of displaying a caller name under the described rules.
Key Points
  • 01India will require telecom service providers to display a caller's registered name with the caller's number for incoming calls on 4G and newer networks beginning November 1, 2026.
  • 02The Department of Telecommunications has directed providers to implement Calling Name Presentation, which shows the caller name recorded in the originating provider's subscriber records.
  • 03If a caller's number is saved in the recipient's contacts, the saved contact name will be shown; otherwise, domestic calls will display the operator-recorded caller name and overseas calls will be labeled "International Call."
  • 04The initial requirement does not cover 2G, 3G, or traditional landline networks, which will be considered separately.
  • 05Providers must offer callers the option to hide their identity, while eligible business and bulk-connection users may use a registered trademark or GST-registered trade name as a preferred name.

An attacker abused Trello’s legitimate invitation system to send a fully authenticated phishing lure impersonating a bank CEO, with attacker-controlled profile and board names embedded in the subject line. A digital bank received a genuine Trello board invitation that impersonated its CEO and used an urgent compliance-themed board title. The attacker created a Trello account with a Proton Mail address, set a display name using the CEO’s name and stylized Unicode “CEO” text, then invited an employee to a board titled “(Attention Needed) Confidential Executive Review: Regulation - Sanction - Compliance.” Trello’s template incorporated the attacker-controlled display name and board title into the email subject line, making the message appear highly credible.

The email was legitimately sent by Trello through Amazon SES and passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks for trello.com. However, the invitation body also displayed the inviter’s Proton Mail address beside the copied executive name, exposing the mismatch between the claimed identity and the account that sent the invitation. The message had no attachment or QR code, and all 16 links led to Trello, Atlassian, or related legitimate pages; it reached one employee and forwarded copies reached three more before an employee reported it. The article advises treating SaaS notification display names and titles as untrusted user-written content, while checking the platform-displayed inviter address as the meaningful identity signal.

  • The Proton Mail plus-address tag matched the target bank’s name, so defenders can search for the base Proton address across their environment while ignoring the tag.
  • All links in the message were legitimate Atlassian-related URLs and scanned clean, showing that link reputation alone would not identify this impersonation lure.
  • The bank’s employee report was the factor that surfaced the message, despite its legitimate delivery infrastructure and clean authentication results.

Why AI Confidence Is Not Validation

TAGSdigital-forensics-ai-investigations-frameworkincident-response-ai-investigations-frameworknistsansscientific-working-group-on-digital-evidence

In plain words

The article argues that AI can help people investigate computer incidents and examine digital evidence, but its confident answers must always be checked by a qualified person. This affects incident responders, forensic examiners, organizations facing security problems, and people whose cases may reach court. If unverified AI claims enter reports or legal testimony, they can lead to incorrect conclusions, while careful records and human oversight help make findings trustworthy.

Summary
AI-generated findings in digital forensics and incident response are not validation: practitioners must independently verify sources, document tools and versions, and retain human authority over irreversible or legally consequential actions.

AI is already used in digital forensics and incident response, but the article argues that a model’s confidence is not proof that its output is correct. AI findings should be traced to the source files and independently verified before they are included in forensic reports, depositions, or court proceedings. SANS says it created separate Digital Forensics & AI Investigations and Incident Response & AI Investigations frameworks to help organizations apply this principle.

The digital-forensics framework is mapped to Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence standards, while the incident-response framework is mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. The article says practitioners should record the tools and versions used, especially for general-purpose models, because AI capabilities may change between an investigation and later testimony. It also distinguishes reversible tasks, such as automated hash verification, from irreversible decisions such as evidence collection or autonomous cloud-data gathering, which should remain under human control.

  • Many examiners may already rely on AI-derived confidence scores through built-in functions such as skin detection, facial similarity, and image categorization even if they say they do not use AI.
  • For AI integrated into a forensic product, naming the product may be sufficient for documentation, but a general-purpose model requires its exact version to be recorded.
  • A single AI policy is unsuitable for both digital forensics and incident response because forensics requires source-by-source validation while incident response may need rapid action during a live event.
  • Human monitoring rather than approval of every action can be workable during an incident when an organization has built and validated the AI making triage or containment recommendations.
  • The article treats reversibility as a practical boundary for AI use: automating hash verification is acceptable, but decisions about evidence collection, cloud-data acquisition, or capturing activity across systems should remain with people.
Key Points
  • 01AI confidence scores are not validation, so investigators must independently confirm AI findings against the original source files before treating them as facts.

In plain words

The article argues that AI tools have changed hiring because applicants can now quickly create long, polished technical reports that once took much more time. This affects employers trying to judge engineers and applicants who may be asked to spend significant unpaid time on assignments. The author says companies should spend less time rewarding lengthy submissions and instead focus on whether a person can check facts, identify what matters, explain their choices, and make sound decisions.

Summary
AI has made polished technical take-home work cheap to produce but costly to verify, weakening it as a hiring signal. Hiring processes should focus less on volume and more on observing candidates' judgment, validation, prioritization, and reasoning.

The author, who hires engineers and researchers at Castle, describes hiring as an information problem in which each stage should reduce a specific uncertainty about a candidate. Traditional signals such as open-source work, technical writing, and take-home assignments can be useful because they historically required meaningful knowledge, effort, or experience to produce. The author argues that companies should avoid assigning expensive work when a shorter conversation could answer the relevant question.

AI has changed the value of polished technical submissions because long analyses of unfamiliar codebases can now be generated much more cheaply, while reviewing and validating them remains costly. The author calls this shift “reverse proof of work,” where production is cheap but verification is expensive, especially when a reviewer must distinguish validated findings from plausible but unimportant suggestions. The article recommends evaluating candidates through shorter exercises and discussions that reveal judgment, prioritization, validation, technical depth, and the ability to explain trade-offs rather than rewarding the volume of material produced.

  • A candidate's use of AI is not inherently a weak signal; building a sophisticated workflow with detailed context and their own technical knowledge can itself demonstrate expertise.
  • The most informative evidence may be what a candidate rejects and why, rather than the number of observations or recommendations they produce.
  • One well-supported observation about a system can reveal more judgment than a long report containing many technically plausible findings.
  • A technically correct improvement may still be unimportant if it does not align with the team's priorities, making prioritization a distinct skill worth evaluating.
  • The article suggests that a discussion of how a candidate validated a claim or defended a recommendation can provide more useful evidence than a lengthy take-home deliverable.
Key Points
  • 01The author views hiring as an information problem in which each interview step should reduce a specific uncertainty about the candidate and role fit.
  • 02Traditional hiring signals such as take-home assignments can be useful when they are difficult to fake, because a candidate's effort can reveal knowledge or experience.
  • 03AI-assisted reports can be quick to generate but expensive for hiring managers to assess, because the final document does not clearly show what the candidate independently discovered, validated, or refined.
  • 04The author calls this shift "reverse proof of work," where producing a polished artifact becomes cheap while verifying its usefulness and origin remains costly.
  • 05The article recommends shorter exercises and follow-up discussions that assess candidates' judgment, prioritization, validation, technical depth, and explanation of trade-offs rather than rewarding the volume of material produced.

Constella promotes predictive security as a way to use breached and infostealer-derived identity data alongside internal access context to identify and remediate likely attack paths before intrusion is detected. The approach prioritizes actions such as credential resets, session reviews, device investigation, and monitoring for exposed high-risk accounts.

Constella Intelligence describes predictive security as using evidence of stolen identities, credentials, and other exposed information to identify likely opportunities for attackers before an intrusion is confirmed. The article says breach data and infostealer logs can show what information may already be in adversaries’ hands. Organizations can combine this external exposure intelligence with internal knowledge about account status, access privileges, authentication controls, and business impact. This helps teams decide which exposures require the fastest response.

In the article’s illustrative scenario, infostealer malware on a finance employee’s personal laptop captures credentials associated with the employee’s corporate email address while the employee accesses a browser-based business application. After Constella identifies the exposure, the security team investigates the device, resets credentials, reviews active sessions, checks recent activity, and assesses access privileges and authentication controls. The article emphasizes acting before there is proof that an attacker used the information, rather than waiting for internal monitoring to detect unauthorized access. It recommends assigning ownership for findings, defining response criteria, and tracking assessment and remediation times, unresolved high-priority exposures, and repeated exposure involving the same identities.

paru tool

patching concept

phishing lures technique

phishing messages technique

phishing sites concept

phone numbers concept

physical consequence concept

Private AI Compute product
Google's protected computing environment for analyzing certain data with AI while aiming to limit access to it.
private key concept

private sector organization

A U.S. law that sets rules for certain investor lawsuits and disclosures about future-looking business statements.
privilege-escalation technique

privileges concept

public sector organization
Government organizations and publicly funded services.
public services concept

Python is a popular programming language often used to write scripts, automation tools, and security research code.
also: python3, Python subprocesses

QA, short for quality assurance, is the process of testing software to find problems before it is released.
qilin

Reasoning is the process of working through information logically to reach an answer or decision.

recommendation concept

Red Hat organization

redirect concept

resilience concept

A cybersecurity company that provides data backup, recovery, and data-security products.
run code concept
